caseno: Appeal from Original Order No. 40 of 1978
lawyer:
S. R. Pal with S. S. Halder & A. Y. Masihuzzaman ----- For the Appellant
Aminul Huq ----- For the Respondent No. 1
A .K.M. Shafiqur Rahman with Mustafa Niaz Mohammad ----- For the Respondent No. 2
parties:
Kazi Abdul Khaleque ----- Appellant
Vs.
Kazi Fazlur Rahman and ors ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
2. Facts leading to this appeal, in brief, are that respondent No. 1, (hereinafter called the respondent) as petitioners filed a complaint under Article 36 of the Bar Council Act, 1965 on 16.6.1970. The respondent who was the then Managing Director of Alijan Jute Mills was a friend of the appellant who was appointed Legal Advisor of Alijan Jute Mills by the respondent. It has been alleged that Mr. Kazi Abdul Khaleque represented himself as an Advocate to the respondent and a letter of appointment was issued in his favour on 1.1.66 appointing him as the Legal Advisor of Alijan Jute Mills and fixing his retainer fee at Taka 2,400.00 per annum @ Taka 200.00 per month and court attendance fee at Taka 50.00 per case per day. According to the Respondent the appellant was paid Taka 29,000.00 upto 18.12.68 on account of fees for conducting cases mostly in the Labour Court as per bills appellant attending submitted by him. Although the regularly submitted his bills for court case he never submitted his bill for his retainer fee till that time. All on a sudden in letter dated 14.12.68 addressed to the respondent, the appellant for the first time mentioned that his retainer fee was Taka 1200.00 per month and the court attendance fee was Taka 250.00 per case per day. The petitioner was taken aback by this fantastic claim and searched for the office copy of the letter of appointment but it was found missing from the office file. The respondent then requested the appellant to show him the original letter of appointment issued to him but the appellant did not comply with the request. On the contrary he filed a petition before the then Martial Law Court No. III at Dacca for realisation of his retainer fee of Taka 49,200.00 @ Taka 1200.00 per month from 1.1.66 to 31.5.69. The respondent being served with notice, duly appeared before the Martial Law Court and there he was compelled to pay under duress and threat the amount of Taka 30,000.00 to the appellant in order to avoid further harassment. According to the respondent, the appellant filed a photostat copy of a letter dated 1.1.66 in support of his claim before the Martial Law Court. The respondent, however, with the permission of the Martial Law Court took two photostat copies from that photostat copy filed by the appellant and found to his utter surprise that the letter of appointment dated 1.1.66 has been interpolated by putting the figure before the original figure '200' and the figure `2' before the original figure '50' and the figure 2400 was changed to 14,000 by over typing. The respondent got the photostat copy examined by a Hand Writing Expert and submitted the photostat copy and the opinion of the Expert along with the petition of complaint before the Bar Council. The respondent further alleged that the appellant gave himself out as a full-fledged advocate long before his enrollment as an Advocate of the Dacca District Court and ever since his appointment as Legal Adviser on 1.1.66 the appellant has been representing himself as an Advocate of the Dacca High Court in his letters and bills though he was actually enrolled as an Advocate of the High Court only on 1.8.1969. He thus secured his appointment by false representation and extorted from the respondent by fraudulent interpolation, coercion and intimidation money which were not his legal dues. 

 12. Under Order 6, rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure no pleading except by way of amendment, shall raise any new ground of claim or contain any allegation of fact inconsistent with the previous pleadings of the party pleading the same. According to the aforesaid provision of law after the parties have filed their pleadings they will not be allowed to depart from the pleadings or raise any new allegations of fact inconsistent with the previous pleadings. If any addition or alteration is sought or desired, the party may apply for amendment under Order 6, rule 17 of the Code or an additional statement may be filed under Order 8, rule 9 of the Code. The Court will, however, not allow any party to make out a new case not made out in the written objection. The appellant, therefore, cannot be allowed to blow hot and cold at the same time. The genuineness of the photostat copy of the letter of appointment filed by the respondent was never challenged by the appellant in his written objection and it is on record as Annexure-A to the petition of complaint filed by the respondent. Since this is on record without any challenge from the appellant, we take judicial notice of the same. We have ourselves looked into the consistent case of the respondent that the delinquent Advocate was appointed as a Legal Adviser at a retainer fee at Taka 200.00 per month and Taka 50.00 as court attendance fee per day per case, whereas it has been the case of the appellant that he was appointed legal adviser at retainer fee at the rate of Taka 1200.00 per month and Taka 250.00 per case per day for court attendance fee. The appellant bad not only been claiming this rate of fees but he bad actually gone to the Martial Law Court to realise his fees on the basis of this rate which has although been challenged by the respondent. There is no doubt that there have been interpolations in the photocopy that is before us. Even to a naked eye, it is apparent that the figure was put before the '200.00' to make it '1200' and the figure 2 has been put before the figure '50' to make it '250'. Besides, there was clear over typing on the figure "400  to change it to 1,000 Now, not only this allegation has been made consistently by the respondent, there are certain attending circumstances which also go to lend support to this very serious allegation. If we recall the background of the case that on 1.1.66 the appellant was appointed as the Legal Adviser of the Alijan Jute Mill when, admittedly, he was then not even enrolled as an Advocate of the District Court far less of the High Court. He was enrolled as an Advocate of the District Court on 3.1.66 and as an Advocate of the then High Court of East Pakistan on 1.8.68 but in his own letter dated 14.12.68 addressed to the respondent, the appellant had represented himself as a lawyer since middle of 1965. The relevant portion of the letter was as follows: 

 There is no earthly reason why an established firm like a Jute Mill would go for a new lawyer to be appointed as a Legal Adviser when certainly there was no dearth of lawyers around. Evidently, his relationship with the respondent being his classmate and friend from long before, helped him to get the appointment. It must be remembered that be was just a beginner in his profession on 3.1.66 and in those good old days in 1966 when the real value of money had not gone down to the extent it has today, Taka 1200.00 as retainer fee per month and Taka 250.00 for court attendance fee per day, is an amount which would have been the envy of any Senior lawyer practicing at that time. The appellant does deny the interpolations but says that the respondent had interpolated his letter of appointment for collateral purposes. We asked Mr. Pal, a simple question. To whose bonnet does the interpolated inflated figures endure to the respondent or to the appellant? Furthermore, the alterations and interpolations in the letter of appointment is in perfect harmony with the claim that the appellant has been consistently making although and is possibly the reason why he did not challenge the genuineness of the photostat copy submitted by the Respondent before the Tribunal at any stage of the proceeding or in his written objection. Probably it was in the mind of the appellant that if a photo copy was taken, then the interpolations in the original would not reveal themselves as clearly as in the original. The facts and circumstances of this unfortunate case reveal that the appellant had been working on the plan for quite long and what is most unfortunate in this case was that the respondent being his friend and classmate had really gone all out to establish him as a lawyer but in return the appellant had choosen to bite the hand that fed him. He is not only guilty of gross professional misconduct, but his conduct was grossly in-human. He went to the Martial Law Court for extorting money on threat. It is rather intriguing that being a lawyer himself the appellant had thought it appropriate to seek the protection of the Martial Law Court for settlement of a dispute which was essentially a professional and civil dispute. There he found a ready accomplice in D.W.I, Major Harunur Rashid who in his evidence has come out with a story which the appellant himself did not say. Peculiarly enough nowhere in his written objection the appellant says a word about the presence of Major Harunur Rashid before the Martial Law Court or even his alleged mediation. P.W. 6 Mujaffar Hussain, a responsible Police Officer who was deputed to the Martial Law Court at the relevant time has come out with a credible evidence. Mr. Muzaffar Hussain has denied that the respondent was ever arrested by the Martial Law Court or that there was any mediation by Major Harunur Rashid or that he was ever present in the Martial Law Court nor was Mr. Hussain cross-examined about Major Harunur Rashid. He denied that any forged receipt was produced by the respondent before the Martial Law Court about which D.W.I Harunur Rashid had stated in his evidence. Major Harunur Rashid indeed displayed photogenic memory when he gave detailed description of events and incidents in 1969 while deposing before the Tribunal in July 1977 which was indeed an incredible human feat. 

 13. As stated earlier, 9 witnesses were examined for the petitioner-respondent while 2 witnesses were examined by the appellant including himself. PW.I. is a formal witness who deposed that the appellant was enrolled as an Advocate in the then High Court of East Pakistan on 1.8.68. P.W.2 was the Ex-Accountant of the Aljan Jute Mills who proved the bills submitted by the appellant and deposed that the appellant did not submit any bill for his retainer fees. P.W. 3 was the Legal Assistant of the Alijan Jute Mills who stated that be filed the petition of complaint on behalf of the petitioner. The petition was drafted by the then Secretary Mr. Qusim and was lying with him He further stated that the office file relating to this complaint was missing since 9th December, 1971. P.W.4 is the Secretary of the Alijan Jute Mills who proved the letter dated 5th August, 1972 addressed by the appellant to the Bangladesh Jute. Mills Corporation. PW 5 is the Auditor of Hanglahesh Jute Mills Corporation who deposed that normally the retainer fee of lawyers of different Jute Mills varied from Taka 2017/- to Taka 500.00 per month. P.W.6. is the Additional Superintendent of Police Dacca who in 1969 at the relevant time was the Police Liason Officer of the Martial Law Court. He was present in that Court when the appellant filed the complaint and on being asked by Captain Faruque, the Army Officer, settled the matter and further stated that the respondent in order to avoid further trouble and harassment agreed to pay Taka 30,000;00 to the appellant. He also deposed that he found interpolations in the photostat copy before the Military Court. He categorically dented that any receipt was produced by the respondent and further denied that he was asked by Captain Faruque to arrest the respondent. This witness categorically stated that he did not know the respondent but knew the appellant who was his neighbour. P.W.7. is the petitioner-respondent himself who stated in details about the complaint case as already stated above. He further submitted that the appellant submitted the photostat copy of his appointment letter before the Military Court and he took two photostat copies from there duly attested by one of the army officers and proved the photostat copy he filed before the Tribunal. He has further stated that both he and the appellant got admitted in the Intermediate class in Jagannath Collage from where they passed intermediate and B.A. Examinations together. He further stated that he had to pay Taka 30,000.00 to the appellant out of fear. P.W. 8 is the Hand Writing Expert. P.W. 9 is the Inspector of Police, C.I.D., Dacca. He produced the office records and proved the opinion of the Hand Writing Expert furnished at the instance of the Alijan Jute Mills and proved the signature of the Hand Writing Expert.
